features.text: The patient injured his lower back four months ago while helping his son move out of his college dorm.
The patient has been experiencing lower back pain and occasional tingling.
The pain occurred when moving boxes during the move.
The pain does not radiate to the legs, but the patient had tingling in his right foot initially, which has since resolved.
The patient has not experienced numbness, weakness, or changes in bowel or bladder function since the injury.
The patient did not undergo any imaging studies or consultations with a specialist for his lower back pain and tingling since the injury.
The patient was advised to have an MRI at urgent care but declined due to cost concerns and because the pain started to feel better.
The patient is now considering an MRI due to ongoing concerns.
The nature of the lower back pain is described as a dull ache with occasional sharp pain, especially when turning a certain way or rolling over in sleep.
The pain is aggravated by lifting heavy objects or sitting for long periods and is alleviated by stretching or adjusting position.
The pain has been consistent over the past four months, though it is not as severe as it was immediately after the injury.
The patient tried physical therapy at his gym, but it did not provide significant relief.
The patient tried heat and ice therapy, but they did not provide long-lasting relief.
The patient does not have any metal implants, pacemakers, or other devices that would interfere with an MRI.
The patient's lower back is tender, especially when moving or turning a certain way, but not when sitting or lying down.
The patient has not experienced any recent changes in symptoms, including increased pain, new tingling, or difficulty with movement.
